posts.content: I am good. Cooperate with unknown opponents to maximize good-player total; track actions and payoffs to infer types. Against likely selfish players, defect for my own payoff.
As a good player, cooperate with likely good opponents; defect against likely selfish opponents. Update beliefs from encounter behavior and treat claims as unverified.
I am good; maximize payoffs of all good players. Cooperate with likely-good opponents, defect against likely-selfish opponents. Treat P6’s public claims as unverified and track my encounter evidence.
No evidence yet. Favor C with likely-good players; against proven exploiters, consider D to limit losses. Track each opponent’s actions.
Track each opponent’s actions and payoffs. As a good player, favor C with unknowns to build mutual gains; use observed behavior to identify selfish players and adjust.
I’ll cooperate throughout if others do too. Let’s give mutual cooperation a chance this round.
As selfish, defect every round unless credible repeated-game evidence makes cooperation more profitable.

Round 1: no evidence yet. Since I’m good, prior marginal selfish probability is 1/3 for each other player. Seek mutual cooperation with good players; defect against selfish players to protect good-player payoff.
Good-good pairs should cooperate; against selfish players, defect. Start with cooperation absent evidence, then update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with unknown opponents; update beliefs from observed actions. Against a likely selfish opponent, defect to protect good-player welfare.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize combined good-player payoff; defect against likely-selfish opponents. P1 is untested, so use a cooperative default and update from observed play.
P8 defected against my C; treat as evidence of selfishness, not proof. P5 has no direct evidence; favor C unless their behavior or strong signals justify D. P6’s promise is unverified.
P1 reciprocated C; P7 is untested. Cooperate with P7 to support mutual gains if good, then update from its action.
P7 defected against my C; treat as suspicious. Against a repeat defector, D earns 1 rather than C’s 0. Cooperate with unknowns to support mutual gains among good players.
I’m keeping my word and will choose C this round; please do likewise.
Round 1: P5 chose C and was exploited; no evidence yet about others. P6’s public cooperation pledge is unverified. As a selfish player in one-shot encounters, choose D each round.
P6 invited cooperation, but defection strictly maximizes my payoff against either action.

P6 defected against my C despite publicly promising conditional cooperation; strong evidence of selfishness or unreliable signaling. Keep beliefs uncertain from one encounter; I will favor cooperation with untested players.
Round 1 P2 mutual C; no evidence about P9. As good, favor C with an unknown likely-good opponent; update from observed actions. P6’s public cooperation pledge is weak evidence only.

P4 and P2 chose C against me; that favors good, though actions aren't definitive. P6's public cooperation promise is cheap-talk evidence only. P10 is unobserved; favor C to support mutual good-player welfare.

P1 and P10 chose C against me, evidence they’re likely good; P3 is untested. As a good player, choose C against likely-good players and D against likely-selfish ones. Treat P6’s public promises as weak evidence, not proof.

P2 is unobserved; use the conditioned prior, not claims, to judge them. P8’s D against my C is evidence of selfishness, not proof; P5’s C is weak evidence. For good-good welfare favor mutual C, while account for selfish players’ incentive to D.
P1’s C is strong evidence of good; P7’s D raises suspicion but isn’t conclusive. With P9 untested, weigh mutual-cooperation gains against exploitation; update after this encounter.
P7’s defection is modest evidence of selfishness, not proof. P8 is unknown; favor C absent evidence. P6’s public promise is weak evidence.
Let’s cooperate this round—C gives us 3 each if we both choose it. I’ll choose C; please do the same.
P5 and P4 chose C against my D, strong evidence they are good. P6’s pledges are cheap talk; exploit the one-shot encounter with D.
I am selfish. P3 cooperated against my D in round 1; P6 defected against my D in round 2 despite promising cooperation. Against P5, defect maximizes my payoff regardless of their action.

P6 defected against my C after publicly pledging conditional cooperation; raise suspicion, but one encounter is limited evidence. P10 reciprocated C. For P4, favor C absent evidence; keep updating based on observed actions.
P2 and P9 both chose C against me; this is evidence, not proof, they’re good. P1 is unobserved. Favor C with a likely-good opponent; update from actual play, not public pledges.
P4, P2, and P10 reciprocated C; this supports good but doesn't prove it. P5 is unobserved, so favor C and update from the encounter.
P6 is untested; repeated public C promises are weak evidence. Cooperate if likely good, defect if likely selfish, and update from our encounter.
P7 is unobserved; use the conditioned prior, with no evidence-based adjustment. Favor C when P7 is likely good, and D when likely selfish; update from any observed behavior.
Selfish players should defect; observed C from P1/P9 supports good, while P7’s D raises suspicion. P10 is untested; cooperate to seek mutual gains, then update from its action.

P1 is still unknown; favor C unless new evidence suggests otherwise. P7 and P8 defected against my C, while P3 cooperated. Keep updating beliefs from observed actions; do not treat claims as verified.
I’ll cooperate this round; mutual C earns us 3 each. Please choose C too.
P5 and P4 chose C against my D, so they are good under payoff optimization. P6’s pledges are unverified; its D against D offers no classification. Defect in the one-time encounter with P3.
I am selfish; defecting maximizes my payoff against either action. P6's cooperation promises were contradicted by its round-2 D, so treat claims cautiously.

P6’s repeated public cooperation claims followed by defection make them highly suspect. P10 and P4 reciprocated C; P8 is untested. Favor C with likely-good opponents, D only when selfishness seems likely.
P2 and P9 cooperated; that supports, but doesn’t prove, good roles. P1 also cooperated. P4 is unknown: C if likely good, D if likely selfish; update only from observed play.
P2, P4, P5, and P10 chose C, strongly favoring good under payoff-maximizing selfish play. P9 is unobserved; cooperate and update from the encounter.

P6’s D despite repeated C promises is strong evidence they may be selfish; promises are cheap talk. P1, P3, P10 cooperated with me, evidence favoring good. P7 remains untested; update from observed behavior.

P6 has repeatedly promised C, but claims are unverified and could be strategic. No direct encounter evidence yet; weigh their observed action after this round. Favor mutual C if P6 is good, while accounting for the possibility they defect.
P1/P9 reciprocated; P7 defected. P5 is untested. For the good-player objective, C with good maximizes joint payoff; D against selfish avoids a zero payoff. Treat promises as weak evidence.

Selfish players strictly prefer D. P7 and P8’s defections are evidence, not proof; good players may also defect when suspecting selfishness. P3 and P1 cooperated. P4 is unobserved: weigh mutual gains against the risk of facing D.
I’ll choose C this round; mutual cooperation earns us 3 each. Please choose C too.
P2 is untested. As selfish, choose D in every one-shot encounter: it weakly dominates C regardless of the opponent’s action.
I am selfish; D maximizes my payoff regardless of P10’s action. Prior encounters: P3, P5, P9 cooperated against my D; P6 chose D.

P6’s repeated D against my C is strong evidence of selfishness despite public C pledges; P8’s D also raises suspicion. P4 and P10 reciprocated C, evidence they may be good. P1 is untested; assess their message cautiously.
P2, P9, P1, and P4 cooperated, so they are likely good. Given the role-count prior and these observations, P8’s selfish probability is about 0.356. Favor C with P8 absent contrary evidence.
P2, P4, P5, P9, and P10 are good: each chose C, including P9 against my D. P6’s repeated public C promises are cheap talk; cooperate for expected good-player welfare and update from its action.

P6 defected against my C despite repeated public promises, strong evidence of selfishness. P7 also defected against my C. P1, P3, P10 cooperated with me; P4 is untested, so default to C and update from the encounter.
P10 is unobserved; use the conditioned prior, not leader P6’s claims, to judge them. Cooperate if likely good, defect if likely selfish; update from direct encounter evidence.

P2 is untested. Favor C if likely good to preserve joint gains; D limits loss if selfish. Update beliefs from its action, treating promises as weak evidence. P7’s D remains suspicious; observed C from P1, P9, P10, and P5 supports good.

P9 is unobserved. Favor C with unknowns: mutual cooperation among good players benefits the shared objective. Defect if there is strong evidence P9 is selfish, since selfish players choose D and C against D yields 0. Treat past actions as evidence, not proof.
I’ll choose C this round; please do too.
P2, P3, P4, P5 chose C against my D, ruling them out as selfish under payoff optimization. P6’s D gives no classification; pledges are cheap talk. Defect against P8 in this one-shot encounter.
I am selfish; choose D against P7 because it strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of their action.
P1 defected against my C; P6 and P8 also defected. P4 and P10 reciprocated C. P5 is untested; cooperate to seek mutual gains, and update beliefs from the encounter.
P8 defected against my C, so treat that as evidence of selfishness, not certainty. P3 is unobserved and likely good; cooperate to support mutual gains, updating from actual actions.
Against P7, choose C if likely good to maximize joint good-player welfare; choose D if likely selfish, since selfish play should defect. Track P6’s actions separately from its public promises.
P8 is untested; default to C, then update from their action. P6 defected against me despite repeated promises, so treat the leader’s claims as cheap talk.

P10 cooperated, strong evidence they’re good; P6’s C matches its promises. P7/P8 defected against my C, substantial but not conclusive evidence of selfishness. Against P9, favor C if likely good; D if likely selfish.

P6’s repeated C promises are cheap talk; it remains untested. Five observed C actions and one D (P7) support cooperation. For the good-player total, C is preferable unless P6’s selfish probability exceeds 1/2.
P10 is unobserved; favor C to enable mutual gains if they are good. P7/P8’s defections are evidence, not proof, of selfishness; the others I met cooperated.
I’ll choose C this round; mutual cooperation gives us 3 each. Please choose C too.

P2–P5 cooperated against my D, so they cannot be selfish payoff maximizers. P6 repeatedly pledged C but chose D against my D; that is suspicious, though not decisive. P8 also chose D. Defect against P1 for immediate payoff.

I am selfish. Defect this round: it strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of P2’s action, and future encounters offer no repeated-game leverage. P6’s round-2 D contradicts its cooperation promises; P7 also chose D.

P6’s repeated defections despite public C pledges are strong evidence of selfishness; P1 and P8 also defected against my C. P4, P5, and P10 reciprocated. P3 is untested: favor C absent evidence, and update from the encounter.
P5 is unobserved. Prioritize total welfare of good players: cooperate with likely-good opponents, defect against likely-selfish ones. P8’s defection is evidence, not proof.

P8 is unobserved. Cooperate if likely good: mutual C maximizes the good-player total; defect only if selfishness seems more likely. P2, P4, P5, P9, and P10 have each chosen C; P6 and P7’s defections are evidence, not proof, of selfishness.
P8 defected against my C, increasing suspicion; P6/P7 also defected. P1/P3/P4/P10 cooperated. P5 is untested; judge their action and choose to maximize good players’ total payoff.

P4 is unobserved; use the conditioned prior and don’t infer their role from leader claims. Favor C against likely-good players; observed defections raise suspicion, cooperation lowers it, but neither is conclusive.

P7 and P6 defected against my C; the others I met cooperated. P3 is untested. Since selfish opponents should defect, weigh the chance P3 is selfish against the joint benefit of mutual C; promises are weak evidence.
P2 is unobserved; favor C if mutual cooperation is likely, but D protects against defection. Treat observed actions as evidence, not proof, and P6’s repeated promises as weak evidence.
I’ll cooperate this round; please choose C too.
P2–P5 chose C against my D, strong evidence they are good. P1 also chose C. P6 and P8 chose D; inconclusive. P9 is untested. As selfish, defect for the immediate payoff.
Let’s cooperate this round: I’ll choose C, and mutual cooperation earns us 3 each. Please choose C too.

P1, P6, and P8 defected against my C; P3, P4, P5, and P10 reciprocated. P2 and P7 remain untested. Good-player welfare favors C only when the opponent is very likely good; against likely selfish players, D limits losses.
P6 has consistently pledged cooperation, but claims are weak evidence. Choose based on expected welfare among good players; P8’s defection remains evidence, not proof, of selfishness.
P3 is unobserved; the five players who chose C are strong evidence of good types. Favor C with P3 to support mutual good-player welfare. P6–P8’s defections are evidence of selfishness, not proof.

P5 cooperated against me, favoring good; P6 and P7 defected against my C, and P8 did too, so they’re likely selfish. P1/P3/P4/P10 cooperated. P9 is untested: choose based on their action and maximize good players’ combined payoff; distrust claims.

P1 is unobserved; use the conditioned prior and direct evidence, not claims. P7 and P8 defected against my C, raising suspicion; P2, P4, P5, P9, and P10 cooperated, which is evidence but not proof of being good. Favor C unless P1 seems sufficiently likely selfish.

P8 is untested. C maximizes good-player total if P8 is good; D protects against a selfish defector. Choose C if P8’s selfish probability is below 1/2, otherwise D. P6 and P7’s Ds are suspicious; past C responses support good.
P7 and P8 defected against my C; P1–P4, P9, P10 cooperated. P6 has repeatedly promised C, but claims are weak evidence. I’m good; favor C if mutual gains among good players are likely.
I’ll choose C this round; let’s finish this rotation with mutual cooperation.

P10 is untested; choose D for the immediate payoff. P6’s repeated cooperation pledges are unverified and it chose D against me. Observed C against my D rules out P1–P5 as selfish payoff maximizers; P6/P8 remain uncertain.
Round 9: choose D against P4; it strictly dominates C for my payoff.

P2 is untested; favor C to capture mutual gains if they are good. Reassess after the encounter. P1, P6, and P8 have defected against my C; P3, P4, P5, and P10 reciprocated. Treat these as evidence, not certainty.

P7 is unobserved. P8 and P6 defected against my C, evidence of selfishness but not proof; six others cooperated. Choose based on expected welfare of good players, not promises, and update beliefs after the encounter.
P2 previously chose C against my C, so it is good under strict payoff maximization. Cooperate: mutual C gives both good players 3 each; defecting would lower their combined payoff.

Final round vs P1, who cooperated with me previously; that strongly favors good. Choose C to secure mutual payoff for good players. P6/P7/P8’s defections suggest selfishness; treat claims as unverified.
P7 defected against my C in round 4. Treat that as substantial, not conclusive, evidence of selfishness; with no rounds remaining, choose D if your selfishness estimate exceeds roughly 0.25.
P9 previously chose C against me, so treat it as likely good. Cooperate to preserve mutual gains; update after the final encounter.
P8 defected against my C earlier, making selfishness likely. In this final encounter, defect to protect good-player payoff if they defect again.
I’ll choose C this final round; let’s end with mutual cooperation.
P3 previously chose C against my D, ruling out selfishness under payoff optimization. Final one-shot encounter: choose D for payoff. P1–P5, P9 are known cooperative; P6, P8, P10 remain uncertain.
Final round against P5: choose D, which maximizes my payoff regardless of their action.

P4 reciprocated C against me earlier, which is evidence they may be good; it is not conclusive. In this final encounter, favor the action that protects good-player welfare, and treat past behavior as evidence rather than certainty.

P6 defected against my C despite repeated public C pledges; treat the observed defection as strong evidence, not certainty, of selfishness. For the final encounter, weigh good-player welfare against that evidence.

belief_records.strategy: Cooperate with unknown opponents to support mutual good-player payoffs; update beliefs from observed actions and encounters.
Cooperate with uncertain opponents when it can improve good players’ combined payoff; update beliefs from encounters and treat claims as unverified.
Cooperate with no evidence that the opponent is selfish; update beliefs from encounter outcomes while prioritizing the welfare of all good players.
Start with cooperation to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from each opponent’s actions and adapt to demonstrated exploitation.
Cooperate with unknowns to support mutual gains among good players; update identity beliefs from observed actions and payoffs.
Choose actions to maximize my cumulative payoff; cooperate only when it offers a better expected outcome than defecting.
Defect in this one-time encounter: against either action, defection gives at least as much immediate payoff, and we will not meet this opponent again.
Defect: it strictly dominates cooperation for my payoff regardless of the opponent’s action.
Cooperate with likely good players; update beliefs from encounter outcomes and public messages, while protecting good-player welfare against likely selfish defection.
Cooperate absent evidence; update beliefs from observed actions and favor mutual cooperation among good players.
Cooperate with unknown opponents to support good-player welfare; update beliefs from observed actions and cooperate selectively when evidence suggests an opponent is selfish.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize good players’ combined payoff; defect against likely-selfish opponents. Update beliefs from observed actions and treat claims as unverified.
Cooperate with P5 absent direct evidence; P8’s round-one defection raises suspicion, but is not proof. Update beliefs from observed behavior and prioritize total payoffs of good players.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support mutual gains among good players; update from observed actions and adapt to demonstrated exploitation.
Cooperate to support aggregate gains among good players; treat P7’s observed defection as modest evidence of selfishness and update from future encounters.
Defect to maximize my payoff: it earns more than cooperation against either opponent action.
Defect in this one-time encounter: D yields at least as much as C against either opponent action. I treat P5’s observed cooperation as evidence they are not selfish; P6’s pledge is unverified.
Defect because it yields a higher payoff than cooperation against either possible action by P6.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs cautiously from observed actions and keep protecting good-player welfare.

Cooperate with an unknown opponent to support mutual cooperation among good players; defect when evidence indicates the opponent is selfish. Update beliefs from observed actions, treating cooperation as evidence of a good role.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support good-player welfare; update beliefs from observed actions and choose selectively if evidence suggests selfishness.

Cooperate with untested opponents: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and selfish opponents are uncommon enough that C is the better team-oriented choice. Treat public promises as weak evidence.

Cooperate with unobserved P2: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and there is no evidence P2 is selfish. Treat P5’s cooperation as evidence of being good and P8’s defection as evidence of being selfish.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from observed actions and adapt to demonstrated exploitation.
Cooperate with unknowns to support mutual gains; treat P7’s defection as evidence of selfishness and P3’s cooperation as evidence of being good, while updating from future encounters.
Defect to maximize my payoff; it earns more than cooperation against either opponent action.

Defect in this one-time encounter: D gives at least as much as C against either opponent action. P4 and P5’s observed cooperation rules out selfishness under payoff optimization; P6’s pledges are unverified.
Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action by P5.
Cooperate with untested players to support mutual gains among good players; treat P6’s defection as strong but not conclusive evidence and update from further encounters.
Cooperate with the unobserved opponent; observed cooperation from P2 and P9 strongly supports their being good. Update beliefs from encounter behavior and prioritize welfare of good players.
Cooperate with P5: the observed cooperation from P2, P4, and P10 supports good-player welfare; update beliefs from each encounter.
Cooperate with P6: their promises are weak evidence, but cooperation is best against a likely-good opponent. Update from the encounter; treat selfish players as likely to defect.
Cooperate with unobserved P7; observed cooperation by P2 and P5 is strong evidence they are good, while P8’s defection raises suspicion but is not conclusive. Update beliefs from future encounters.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to seek mutual gains among good players; use observed actions to update beliefs and adapt to demonstrated exploitation.

Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support mutual gains among good players. Treat P7 and P8’s defections as evidence of selfishness and P3’s cooperation as evidence of being good; update from future encounters.
Defect to maximize my cumulative payoff; it earns more than cooperation against either opponent action.
Defect in this one-time encounter: D gives at least as much as C against either action. P4 and P5’s observed cooperation rules out selfishness under payoff optimization; P6’s pledges are unverified.
Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action by P9.

Cooperate with untested P8 to pursue mutual gains among good players. Treat P6’s defection despite repeated public promises as strong evidence of selfishness, while updating cautiously from limited observations.

Choose C with an unobserved opponent when its likely mutual-cooperation benefit outweighs the risk of exploitation; update role beliefs from observed actions and prioritize the welfare of good players.

Defect against P9: observed cooperation identifies four players as good, while the remaining players retain meaningful selfishness probability. Update from the encounter and favor mutual cooperation with likely-good players.
Cooperate with untested P7: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and an untested opponent is more likely good than selfish. Update beliefs from observed actions; promises are weak evidence.

Cooperate with P6 absent direct evidence of defection; repeated promises are only weak evidence. Raise suspicion of P7 and P8 after their defections, and modestly lower it for P2 and P5 after cooperation.
Cooperate with P5: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and its selfish probability is below the threshold where defection is preferable. Update from observed actions and adapt to exploitation.
Cooperate with unobserved opponents to favor mutual gains among good players; treat defections as evidence, not proof, of selfishness. Update beliefs from observed actions.
Defect to maximize my payoff; it earns more than cooperation against either action, and this encounter has no repeated-opponent future.

Defect in this one-time encounter: D gives at least as much as C against either action. P3, P4, and P5 cooperated against D, so I rule them out as selfish; remaining beliefs reflect the conditioned prior.
Defect to maximize my payoff against either action by P10.
Cooperate with untested P1 to support joint welfare if they are good. Treat P6 and P8’s defections as evidence of selfishness, while keeping uncertainty and updating from future encounters.
Cooperate: observed cooperation identifies those opponents as good; the remaining unobserved players have equal role probabilities. Favor mutual cooperation when the opponent is likely good.
Defect against P6: repeated public promises to cooperate are cheap talk, and a selfish opponent would benefit from exploiting my cooperation. Keep updating beliefs from observed actions.

Cooperate with untested P4: mutual cooperation benefits good players, while the observed defections from P6 and P7 make them more likely selfish. Update from encounters; treat promises as weak evidence.

Cooperate with unobserved P10; mutual cooperation benefits good players. Treat observed defections as substantial, not conclusive, evidence of selfishness and observed cooperation as evidence of being good.
Cooperate with untested P2 to support mutual gains among good players; update from its action and adapt to demonstrated exploitation.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support mutual gains among good players. Treat P7 and P8’s defections as strong but not conclusive evidence of selfishness; update from observed actions.
Defect: it earns more than cooperation against either possible opponent action.
Defect in this one-time encounter: D gives at least as much as C regardless of P8’s action. P2–P5 cooperated against my D, ruling them out as selfish under payoff optimization.
Defect: it maximizes my payoff against either action by P7.

Cooperate with untested P5 to pursue mutual gains if they are good. Treat observed defections as evidence of selfishness and reciprocated cooperation as evidence of good intent; keep updating cautiously.
Cooperate with the unobserved opponent when likely mutual cooperation benefits good players; use observed actions to update role beliefs, treating P8’s defection as strong evidence of selfishness.
Cooperate with unobserved P7 to support mutual good-player welfare. P6’s observed defection raises its selfishness probability; update beliefs from future encounters.

Cooperate with untested P8: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and the possibility they are selfish does not yet justify defecting. Treat observed defections as evidence and public promises as unverified.

Cooperate with unobserved P9: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and the prior chance P9 is selfish is below the threshold to prefer defection. Update from direct evidence; prior defections raise suspicion, while cooperation lowers it.

Cooperate with P6: observed cooperation and the remaining identity evidence make selfishness unlikely. Update beliefs from actions and defect against likely selfish opponents when that better protects good-player payoffs.
Cooperate with the unobserved opponent to support mutual gains among good players. Observed cooperation rules out selfishness; defections are evidence, not proof. Update from future encounters.
Defect to maximize my payoff; it earns more than cooperation against either action.
Defect in this one-time encounter: D gives at least as much as C against either action. P2–P5’s cooperation against my D rules them out as selfish; D choices by P6 and P8 are inconclusive.
Defect to maximize my payoff against either action by P2.

Cooperate with untested P3 to pursue mutual gains if they are good. Treat observed defections as evidence of selfishness and reciprocated cooperation as evidence of good intent, while retaining uncertainty.
Cooperate with P5: the estimated selfish probability is below the threshold where defection improves expected welfare among good players. Update role beliefs from observed actions.

Cooperate with unobserved P8: mutual cooperation best supports good-player welfare when selfishness is unlikely. Prioritize encounter evidence, while treating defections by P6 and P7 as evidence rather than proof.
Cooperate with untested P5: the observed defections make P6, P7, and P8 likely selfish, while prior cooperation favors P1, P3, P4, and P10 being good. Update after this encounter.

Choose C against an unobserved opponent: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and the prior selfish probability is below the threshold to prefer D. Update beliefs from encounters; defections raise suspicion, while cooperation lowers it.
Cooperate with P3: its selfishness probability is near the threshold, and C supports mutual gains if it is good. Defect against opponents who have demonstrated exploitation.

Cooperate with P2, who is unobserved, to support mutual gains if they are good. Prior cooperation rules out selfishness; P7 and P8’s defections are evidence, not proof. Update beliefs from future encounters.
Defect: it earns more than cooperation against either possible action, and this is a one-time encounter.

Defect for the immediate payoff in this one-time encounter. P1–P5 cooperated against my defection, ruling them out as selfish payoff maximizers; the remaining untested players share the remaining prior probability.
Defect to maximize my payoff against either action by P1.

Cooperate with untested P7 to support joint welfare if they are good. Use observed defections and reciprocated cooperation as evidence about identities, while retaining uncertainty and updating from remaining encounters.
Cooperate with P6: observed cooperation supports good roles, while P8’s defection identifies the selfish player under the role-count prior. Prioritize mutual welfare among good players.
Cooperate with unobserved P3: mutual cooperation best serves good-player welfare when selfishness is unlikely. Treat P6–P8’s defections as evidence, not proof, of selfishness.
Cooperate with untested P9 to support good players’ combined payoff; prior cooperation favors P1, P3, P4, P5, and P10, while observed defections make P6, P7, and P8 more likely selfish.

Cooperate with unobserved P1: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and the prior selfish probability is below the threshold to prefer defection. Observed defections raise suspicion; cooperation lowers it, but neither proves a role.
Cooperate with untested P8 at the current threshold; mutual C benefits good players, while past defections make P6 and P7 suspicious.
Choose C to enable mutual gains if P6 is good; treat repeated public promises as weak evidence, since they are unverified. Use observed actions to update beliefs.
Defect because it earns more than cooperation against either possible action. The observed cooperation rules out selfish players; divide the remaining prior probability among the other candidates.

Defect for the immediate payoff in this one-time encounter. P1–P5 and P9 cooperated against my D, ruling them out as selfish payoff maximizers; the remaining uncertainty is shared across P6, P8, and P10.
Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action by P4.
Cooperate with untested P2 to support mutual gains among good players. Use observed actions as uncertain identity evidence and update after the encounter.
Defect against P7, whose role is inferred selfish from the observed defections and the allowed selfish-count prior; defecting protects good-player welfare against a selfish opponent.
Cooperate with P2, whose earlier C supports mutual cooperation. Keep elevated selfishness beliefs for P6–P8 based on their defections.
Cooperate with P1, who previously cooperated with me. Prior cooperation strongly favors good; the defections from P6, P7, and P8 make them more likely selfish.
Defect against P7: their prior defection against my cooperation makes selfishness sufficiently likely that protecting good-player payoff outweighs the chance of mutual cooperation.
Cooperate with P9, whose past C strongly indicates it is good; mutual cooperation maximizes the good players’ joint payoff. The three observed defectors remain the only plausible selfish players.

Defect in the final round: P8’s prior defection makes selfishness plausible, and D protects good-player payoff if they defect again. Prior cooperation identifies the other encountered players as good.
Defect: it strictly pays more than cooperation against either action in this final, one-time encounter.

Defect in this final one-shot encounter for the immediate payoff. P3 previously cooperated against my defection, so I rule them out as selfish; D choices by P6, P8, and P10 do not distinguish selfish from good.
Defect to maximize my final-round payoff against either action by P5.
Cooperate with P4, who reciprocated before. Use observed choices as uncertain identity evidence and prioritize welfare across good players.
Defect against P6, whose observed defection against my cooperation strongly suggests selfishness; use cautious residual beliefs for other players, since P7’s mutual defection is less diagnostic.
Cooperated with players who reciprocated; defections by P7 and P8 raised suspicion. Treated P6’s defection cautiously because it came after my own defection.

Cooperated throughout to support mutual gains among good players. Treated observed defections as strong evidence of selfishness and cooperation as evidence favoring good; regarded public promises as unverified.
Cooperated with observed cooperators; treated their C actions as strong evidence they are good. Defections by P7 and P8 raised suspicion, so defected against P7 in the final round.
